title: Mass & Energy Analysis of Control Volumes

problems.title: Mass flow rate in a pipe
problems.scenario:
Water ($\rho = 1000\ \text{kg/m}^3$) flows through a pipe of diameter **5.0 cm** at an average velocity of **3.0 m/s**.

Find the **mass flow rate**, in kg/s.
hints: $\dot m = \rho V A$, with $A = \pi D^2/4$.
problems.solution:
The cross-sectional area:

$$A = \frac{\pi D^2}{4} = \frac{\pi(0.05)^2}{4} = 1.963\times10^{-3}\ \text{m}^2$$

Then the mass flow rate:

$$\dot m = \rho V A = 1000 \times 3.0 \times 1.963\times10^{-3} = 5.89\ \text{kg/s}$$

problems.title: Velocity from mass flow
problems.scenario:
Air with specific volume $v = 0.80\ \text{m}^3/\text{kg}$ flows at $\dot m = 0.50\ \text{kg/s}$ through a duct of cross-sectional area **0.010 m²**.

Find the **average velocity**, in m/s.
hints: $\dot m = VA/v$. Rearrange for $V$.
$V = \dot m\,v / A$.
problems.solution:
Starting from $\dot m = \dfrac{VA}{v}$ and solving for velocity:

$$V = \frac{\dot m\,v}{A} = \frac{0.50 \times 0.80}{0.010} = \frac{0.40}{0.010} = 40\ \text{m/s}$$

Using specific volume here is handy because gas tables list $v$ directly.

problems.title: Nozzle exit velocity
problems.scenario:
Steam enters an adiabatic nozzle at **30 m/s**, and its specific enthalpy drops by **20 kJ/kg** as it accelerates.

Find the **exit velocity**, in m/s. (Neglect potential energy; no work.)
hints: For a nozzle ($\dot W = 0$, adiabatic): $h_1 + V_1^2/2 = h_2 + V_2^2/2$.
Rearrange: $V_2 = \sqrt{V_1^2 + 2(h_1 - h_2)}$.
Convert the enthalpy drop to J/kg: $20\ \text{kJ/kg} = 20\,000\ \text{J/kg}$.
problems.solution:
A nozzle trades enthalpy for kinetic energy with no work and no heat:

$$h_1 + \frac{V_1^2}{2} = h_2 + \frac{V_2^2}{2} \quad\Rightarrow\quad V_2 = \sqrt{V_1^2 + 2(h_1 - h_2)}$$

With $h_1 - h_2 = 20\,000\ \text{J/kg}$ (note the unit conversion — enthalpy in **J/kg** to match $V^2$ in m²/s²):

$$V_2 = \sqrt{(30)^2 + 2(20\,000)} = \sqrt{900 + 40\,000} = \sqrt{40\,900} = 202.2\ \text{m/s}$$

problems.title: Adiabatic steam turbine power
problems.scenario:
Steam enters an adiabatic turbine at $h_1 = 3248\ \text{kJ/kg}$ and leaves at $h_2 = 2378\ \text{kJ/kg}$, with mass flow $\dot m = 3.0\ \text{kg/s}$. Neglect kinetic and potential energy.

Find the **power output**, in kW.
hints: For an adiabatic turbine with negligible KE/PE: $\dot W = \dot m(h_1 - h_2)$.
Just substitute the enthalpies and mass flow.
problems.solution:
The steady-flow energy equation for an adiabatic turbine (no heat, negligible KE/PE) reduces to:

$$\dot W = \dot m\,(h_1 - h_2) = 3.0 \times (3248 - 2378) = 3.0 \times 870 = 2610\ \text{kW}$$

The enthalpy drop across the turbine is what becomes shaft work.

problems.title: Pump power for a liquid
problems.scenario:
A pump raises the pressure of water from **100 kPa** to **5000 kPa** at $\dot m = 10\ \text{kg/s}$. Water's specific volume is $v = 0.001\ \text{m}^3/\text{kg}$.

Find the **pump power**, in kW.
hints: A liquid's specific volume barely changes, so $\Delta h \approx v\,\Delta P$.
$\dot W_{pump} = \dot m\,v\,(P_2 - P_1)$.
$\text{kg/s} \times \text{m}^3/\text{kg} \times \text{kPa} = \text{kW}$.
problems.solution:
For an (incompressible) liquid the pump's enthalpy rise is essentially $v\,\Delta P$, giving the shortcut:

$$\dot W_{pump} = \dot m\,v\,(P_2 - P_1) = 10 \times 0.001 \times (5000 - 100)$$

$$\dot W_{pump} = 10 \times 0.001 \times 4900 = 49\ \text{kW}$$

This avoids needing compressed-liquid enthalpy tables — a big practical time-saver.

problems.title: Throttling valve — exit quality
problems.scenario:
Refrigerant R-134a, saturated liquid at **0.80 MPa** ($h_1 = 95.47\ \text{kJ/kg}$), is throttled to **0.12 MPa**. At 0.12 MPa, $h_f = 22.49$ and $h_{fg} = 214.48\ \text{kJ/kg}$.

Find the **quality** at the valve exit.
hints: A throttling valve is isenthalpic: $h_2 = h_1$.
At the exit pressure the fluid is a mixture, so $h_2 = h_f + x\,h_{fg}$.
Rearrange: $x = (h_2 - h_f)/h_{fg}$.
problems.solution:
Throttling conserves enthalpy ($\dot W = 0$, adiabatic, negligible KE/PE):

$$h_2 = h_1 = 95.47\ \text{kJ/kg}$$

At the downstream pressure the refrigerant is a saturated mixture, so apply the quality relation and rearrange:

$$h_2 = h_f + x\,h_{fg} \quad\Rightarrow\quad x = \frac{h_2 - h_f}{h_{fg}}$$

$$x = \frac{95.47 - 22.49}{214.48} = \frac{72.98}{214.48} = 0.340$$

The sudden pressure drop flashes ~34% of the liquid into vapour — exactly how the expansion valve in a fridge works.

problems.title: Mixing chamber
problems.scenario:
Saturated steam at 100 kPa ($h_1 = 2675\ \text{kJ/kg}$) enters a mixing chamber at $\dot m_1 = 1.0\ \text{kg/s}$ and mixes with cold water at $h_2 = 84\ \text{kJ/kg}$. The mixture leaves at $h_3 = 209\ \text{kJ/kg}$.

Find the **cold-water flow rate** $\dot m_2$, in kg/s. (Adiabatic, no work.)
hints: Mass balance: $\dot m_3 = \dot m_1 + \dot m_2$.
Energy balance: $\dot m_1 h_1 + \dot m_2 h_2 = (\dot m_1 + \dot m_2) h_3$.
Solve for $\dot m_2$: $\dot m_2 = \dot m_1 (h_1 - h_3)/(h_3 - h_2)$.
problems.solution:
Combine the mass balance $\dot m_3 = \dot m_1 + \dot m_2$ with the (adiabatic, no-work) energy balance:

$$\dot m_1 h_1 + \dot m_2 h_2 = (\dot m_1 + \dot m_2)\,h_3$$

Group the $\dot m_2$ terms and solve:

$$\dot m_2 = \dot m_1\,\frac{h_1 - h_3}{h_3 - h_2} = 1.0 \times \frac{2675 - 209}{209 - 84} = \frac{2466}{125} = 19.7\ \text{kg/s}$$

It takes about 20 kg/s of cold water to cool 1 kg/s of steam down to the 209 kJ/kg mixture.
equationsUsed: \dot m_1 h_1 + \dot m_2 h_2 = \dot m_3 h_3

problems.title: Compressor with heat loss
problems.scenario:
Air enters a compressor at $h_1 = 300.19\ \text{kJ/kg}$ and leaves at $h_2 = 503.02\ \text{kJ/kg}$, at $\dot m = 0.20\ \text{kg/s}$. The compressor also **loses 15 kW** of heat to the surroundings. Neglect KE/PE.

Find the **power input** required, in kW.
hints: Energy balance: $\dot Q - \dot W = \dot m(h_2 - h_1)$. Heat loss makes $\dot Q = -15\ \text{kW}$.
Solve for $\dot W$: $\dot W = \dot Q - \dot m(h_2 - h_1)$.
A negative $\dot W$ means work is done *on* the gas — report its magnitude.
problems.solution:
Apply the steady-flow energy balance with $\dot Q = -15\ \text{kW}$ (heat leaves):

$$\dot Q - \dot W = \dot m\,(h_2 - h_1)$$

$$\dot W = \dot Q - \dot m\,(h_2 - h_1) = -15 - 0.20(503.02 - 300.19)$$

$$\dot W = -15 - 0.20(202.83) = -15 - 40.57 = -55.6\ \text{kW}$$

The negative sign confirms work is supplied *to* the compressor, so the **power input is 55.6 kW**. (Both the enthalpy rise *and* the heat loss must be paid for by the shaft work.)

problems.title: Heated air in a pipe (continuity + ideal gas)
problems.scenario:
Air enters a **16 cm**-diameter pipe steadily at **200 kPa, 20°C** with velocity **5 m/s**. It is heated as it flows and leaves at **180 kPa, 40°C**. Take $R = 0.287\ \text{kJ/(kg·K)}$.

Find the **exit velocity**, in m/s.
hints: First find the mass flow rate at the inlet: $\dot m = AV_1/v_1$, with $v_1 = RT_1/P_1$ and $A = \pi D^2/4$.
Mass flow rate is the *same* at exit (steady flow, no branches) — use it to find $V_2$.
$V_2 = \dot m\,v_2/A$, with $v_2 = RT_2/P_2$ at the exit state.
problems.solution:
**Pipe area:**

$$A = \frac{\pi D^2}{4} = \frac{\pi(0.16)^2}{4} = 0.02011\ \text{m}^2$$

**Inlet mass flow rate.** Specific volume at inlet ($T_1=293.15\ \text{K}$):

$$v_1 = \frac{RT_1}{P_1} = \frac{0.287\times293.15}{200} = 0.4207\ \text{m}^3/\text{kg}$$

$$\dot m = \frac{AV_1}{v_1} = \frac{0.02011\times5}{0.4207} = 0.2390\ \text{kg/s}$$

**Exit velocity.** The mass flow rate doesn't change along the pipe. At the exit ($T_2=313.15\ \text{K}$):

$$v_2 = \frac{RT_2}{P_2} = \frac{0.287\times313.15}{180} = 0.4993\ \text{m}^3/\text{kg}$$

$$V_2 = \frac{\dot m\,v_2}{A} = \frac{0.2390\times0.4993}{0.02011} = 5.93\ \text{m/s}$$

Even with a constant-diameter pipe, the velocity **rises** slightly because the heated (less dense) air needs to move faster to pass the same mass through the same area.

problems.title: Adiabatic nozzle: exit area from an ideal gas
problems.scenario:
Air enters an **adiabatic nozzle** steadily at **300 kPa, 200°C, 45 m/s**, with inlet area **110 cm²**, and leaves at **100 kPa, 180 m/s**. Take $R = 0.287\ \text{kJ/(kg·K)}$, $c_p = 1.005\ \text{kJ/(kg·K)}$.

Find the **exit area**, in cm².
hints: First find the inlet mass flow rate from continuity: $\dot m = A_1V_1/v_1$, with $v_1 = RT_1/P_1$.
Adiabatic, no work → the SFEE reduces to $c_p(T_1-T_2) = (V_2^2-V_1^2)/2$. Solve for $T_2$ (watch the kJ vs J unit split).
With $T_2$, get $v_2 = RT_2/P_2$, then $A_2 = \dot m\,v_2/V_2$.
problems.solution:
**Inlet mass flow rate.** With $T_1 = 473.15\ \text{K}$:

$$v_1 = \frac{RT_1}{P_1} = \frac{0.287\times473.15}{300} = 0.4526\ \text{m}^3/\text{kg}$$

$$\dot m = \frac{A_1V_1}{v_1} = \frac{0.0110\times45}{0.4526} = 1.094\ \text{kg/s}$$

**Exit temperature.** Adiabatic and no work, so the SFEE trades enthalpy for kinetic energy:

$$c_p(T_1-T_2) = \frac{V_2^2-V_1^2}{2}$$

$$T_2 = T_1 - \frac{V_2^2-V_1^2}{2\,c_p\times1000} = 473.15 - \frac{180^2-45^2}{2\times1.005\times1000} = 473.15 - 15.11 = 458.0\ \text{K}$$

(dividing by $1000$ converts the $c_p$ term to J so it matches the $V^2$ units).

**Exit area.** Specific volume at exit:

$$v_2 = \frac{RT_2}{P_2} = \frac{0.287\times458.0}{100} = 1.3146\ \text{m}^3/\text{kg}$$

$$A_2 = \frac{\dot m\,v_2}{V_2} = \frac{1.094\times1.3146}{180} = 0.000799\ \text{m}^2 = 79.9\ \text{cm}^2$$

The nozzle narrows even though the gas cools — the huge speed-up (45→180 m/s) dominates over the modest density increase.

problems.title: Steam turbine with kinetic energy included
problems.scenario:
Steam enters an adiabatic turbine at **4 MPa, 500°C** ($h_1 = 3445.3\ \text{kJ/kg}$) with velocity **80 m/s**, and leaves at **30 kPa**, quality **0.92**, velocity **50 m/s**. At 30 kPa: $h_f = 289.23$, $h_{fg} = 2336.1\ \text{kJ/kg}$. Mass flow rate is **12 kg/s**.

Unlike the simpler turbine problem earlier in this chapter, **do not neglect kinetic energy** here. Find the **power output**, in MW.
hints: Find the exit enthalpy from the quality: $h_2 = h_f + x\,h_{fg}$.
This time keep the kinetic-energy term in the SFEE: $w_{out} = (h_1-h_2) + (V_1^2-V_2^2)/2$.
Watch units — $(V_1^2-V_2^2)/2$ comes out in J/kg; divide by 1000 to match $h_1-h_2$ in kJ/kg. Then multiply by $\dot m$.
problems.solution:
**Exit enthalpy** from the given quality:

$$h_2 = h_f + x\,h_{fg} = 289.23 + 0.92\times2336.1 = 2438.4\ \text{kJ/kg}$$

**Specific work**, keeping the kinetic-energy term this time:

$$w_{out} = (h_1-h_2) + \frac{V_1^2-V_2^2}{2} = (3445.3-2438.4) + \frac{80^2-50^2}{2\times1000}$$

$$w_{out} = 1006.9 + 1.95 = 1008.8\ \text{kJ/kg}$$

**Power output:**

$$\dot W = \dot m\,w_{out} = 12\times1008.8 = 12\,106\ \text{kW} = 12.1\ \text{MW}$$

The kinetic-energy correction here is tiny (~0.2% of the total) — but the *skill* of correctly including and unit-converting it, rather than blindly neglecting it, is what this problem tests.
